family_history: No known family history of neurological disease

social_history.living_situation: Lives alone in apartment; adult children nearby
social_history.alcohol: Rare, less than 1 drink per month

patient.chief_complaint: Two-year history of worsening gait instability, urinary incontinence, and gradual cognitive decline
patient.history_present_illness: A 78-year-old retired schoolteacher with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented for inpatient NPH evaluation. Her daughter arranged the admission after noticing her mother's steady functional decline over the past two years. The patient initially attributed her walking difficulties to her knee arthritis, but her orthopedic surgeon noted that her gait pattern was atypical for osteoarthritis — short shuffling steps without significant knee pain during ambulation. She describes her feet as feeling 'stuck to the ground' when she tries to initiate walking. She has fallen four times in the past year, all without loss of consciousness. She now uses a rollator walker for all ambulation. Cognitive changes include increasing difficulty with finances — she accidentally paid the same bill three times in one month — and her daughter reports she repeats questions and has difficulty following complex television programs. She has been managing this independently but admits that she now struggles to follow her daughter's instructions for smartphone use. Urinary incontinence has been present for approximately 18 months; she wears protective pads daily and has stopped attending her church book club due to embarrassment. Her primary care physician obtained a head CT six months ago noting hydrocephalus and referred her for neurology evaluation. She was admitted for comprehensive NPH workup including MRI, lumbar puncture, and tap trial.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. MoCA 20/30. Impaired delayed recall (1/5), executive dysfunction on serial sevens and clock drawing. Processing speed reduced. No aphasia or agnosia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Horizontal and vertical gaze intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Mild symmetric hip flexor weakness (4+/5). No upper extremity weakness. No rigidity or tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild symmetric reduction in vibration sense at ankles bilaterally. Light touch and proprioception intact in hands and feet.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Markedly apraxic with wide base, very short steps (step length approximately 15 cm), reduced foot clearance with shuffling. Freezing on initiation. TUG 32 seconds. 10-meter walk 26 seconds. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test positive — 3 steps back.
neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Snout reflex positive. No nuchal rigidity. Knee crepitus with range of motion but no effusions.

findings.location: high convexity, parasagittal sulci vs Sylvian fissures

signal_characteristics.description: Tight high-convexity sulci with disproportionately enlarged Sylvian fissures
Corpus callosum thinning with upward bowing
Smooth FLAIR caps and halos periventricularly

mri.impression: Florid iNPH imaging: Evans index 0.40, callosal angle 70 degrees, DESH pattern, transependymal periventricular signal, and hyperdynamic aqueductal flow void. Ventriculomegaly markedly disproportionate to cortical atrophy. Clinical correlation recommended.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 13 cmH2O. WBC: 1 cell/mcL (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 38 mg/dL. Glucose: 72 mg/dL (ratio 0.67). cytology: No malignant cells. beta_amyloid_42: 812 pg/mL (normal). total_tau: 184 pg/mL (normal). phospho_tau: 18 pg/mL (normal).

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (42 mL) with quantitative gait assessment

findings.cognitive: MoCA improved from 20 to 23 (3 points at 24h)

findings.urinary: Decreased urgency episodes at 24h post-tap per patient report

specialized_test.impression: Strongly positive tap trial: 34% TUG improvement and 35% 10-meter walk improvement at 24 hours, with 3-point MoCA improvement. Full Hakim's triad response. This is an excellent shunt predictor. Proceed urgently to neurosurgery referral for VP shunt placement.
recommended_actions: Immediate neurosurgery referral for VP shunt
Amyloid PET prior to surgery if cognitive prognosis assessment desired

output.impression: Markedly hyperdynamic aqueductal CSF flow — peak velocity 24 cm/s (normal <18) and stroke volume 88 mcL/cycle (normal <42). Consistent with iNPH pathophysiology. Supports VP shunt candidacy.
Negative amyloid PET. No Alzheimer's amyloid pathology. Cognitive impairment attributable to iNPH. Excellent prognosis for cognitive recovery post-shunting.

Significant improvement in executive function and processing speed post-tap, consistent with frontal-subcortical dysfunction from iNPH. Memory less dramatically improved — likely requires post-shunt recovery time.

findings.finding: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity — involuntary contractions at 120 mL, maximum capacity 200 mL. No evidence of bladder outlet obstruction or intrinsic sphincter deficiency.

output.impression: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity consistent with NPH-related frontal lobe dysfunction. Incontinence is neurogenic, not related to diabetes or other etiology. Expected to improve significantly after VP shunting.

findings.result: Reduced amplitude (4 mcV), borderline conduction velocity — mild distal axonal sensory neuropathy

output.impression: Mild distal sensorimotor neuropathy consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (HbA1c 6.4%). Not sufficient to explain the degree of gait impairment — mild vibratory loss at ankles is attributable to neuropathy but the dominant gait disorder is NPH-related apraxia.

output.query: iNPH tap trial predictive value VP shunt outcomes older adults women

results.title: Gender differences in iNPH presentation and shunt outcomes
results.key_finding: Women with iNPH present slightly older and with more prominent incontinence; shunt outcomes equivalent to men when tap trial is clearly positive

results.title: Evans index and callosal angle as predictors of shunt response
results.key_finding: Evans index >0.38 and callosal angle <75° combined with positive tap trial yield >85% PPV for sustained VP shunt benefit

output.summary: Tap trial TUG improvement >20% combined with Evans index ≥0.38 and callosal angle <75° (as in this patient) yields an excellent prognosis for VP shunt benefit. Negative amyloid PET further optimizes cognitive outcome. Concurrent mild diabetic neuropathy does not preclude VP shunting and does not significantly impact expected gait outcomes.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy causing gait ataxia
differential.key_features: NCS shows mild distal axonal neuropathy consistent with HbA1c 6.4%; however the dominant gait pattern is apraxic/magnetic, not sensory ataxic. NPH is the primary diagnosis.
Normal CSF biomarkers; negative amyloid PET (CL 12); cognitive pattern is frontal-subcortical
Mild periventricular white matter signal; however Evans 0.40 and strongly positive tap trial confirm NPH dominance
Orthopedic surgeon noted atypical gait pattern; NPH gait apraxia confirmed by positive tap trial

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evans index 0.40, callosal angle 70°, DESH, periventricular transependymal signal

optimal_actions.action: Labs (CBC, BMP, HbA1c, TSH, B12, RPR)
High-volume tap trial (42 mL) with pre/post gait analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal OP 13 cmH2O; clearly positive tap (34% TUG improvement)

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET to exclude concurrent Alzheimer's

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Clearly positive tap trial — VP shunt with programmable valve indicated

critical_actions: Confirm Evans index >0.3 and callosal angle <90° on MRI
Confirm normal opening pressure (≤18 cmH2O) at lumbar puncture
Quantify TUG pre- and post-tap — >20% improvement is the key threshold
Refer promptly to neurosurgery given strongly positive tap trial
contraindicated_actions: Attributing gait disorder solely to knee osteoarthritis without workup
Starting cholinesterase inhibitor before ruling out NPH as a reversible cause
Delaying VP shunt referral — functional improvement is time-sensitive
key_reasoning_points: Classic iNPH presentation with florid MRI findings (Evans 0.40, callosal angle 70°, DESH)
Strongly positive tap trial (34% TUG) meets and exceeds the 20% threshold
Negative amyloid PET and normal CSF biomarkers confirm iNPH is the primary diagnosis, not AD
Mild diabetic neuropathy (HbA1c 6.4%) is coincidental — does not explain the dominant apraxic gait
Knee osteoarthritis as a red herring: orthopedic surgeon correctly identified atypical gait pattern

red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral knee osteoarthritis on acetaminophen with gait difficulty
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait impairment attributed to musculoskeletal disease, delaying NPH evaluation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gait is apraxic/magnetic, not pain-limited. Tap trial confirms NPH as primary cause. Orthopedic pathology does not explain wide-based magnetic gait with frontal release signs.

red_herrings.data_point: Diet-controlled type 2 diabetes with mild distal sensory changes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Neuropathic gait attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: NCS shows only mild axonal sensory neuropathy consistent with good glycemic control — insufficient to explain apraxic gait. NPH is the primary etiology.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Straightforward iNPH in a 78-year-old retired schoolteacher — classic triad with florid imaging, strongly positive tap trial. Knee OA and mild diabetic neuropathy as competing red herrings.
